tl;dr: bottom half, starting at step 1.

I often hear phrases like "what's a good thing to practice on guitar?" I don't very often hear the follow-up question of "why," and that makes me sad.

So many new musicians are in such a rush to be good that they end up shooting themselves in the foot with bad and meaningless practice. They rush through their scale drills so they can get to the songs because obviously songs are where the fun is at. However, in rushing through their technique practice they end up never realizing why they're practicing their drills.

If you don't know why you're practicing what you're practicing, you're not practicing to your full potential. Odds are you're not practicing your scales so that one day you can practice your scales faster. You shouldn't be practicing string skipping so that you can get better at practicing string skipping. You practice these things so that when you make music you can make better music. Whether this is playing covers or coming up with your own tunes, practice should have the big-picture goal of making better music.

I went through the music program at a state university, and although they didn't allow guitar as an instrument (the bastards), I was able to choose voice as an instrument. Even still, they didn't teach much modern anything (the bastards), so I ended up singing lots of operatic stuff that I just wasn't really into. But, I wouldn't trade that education for the world (well, maybe an education at Berklee) because it taught me a fantastic method of practicing.

The practice routine I learned comes in three steps: Technique Practice, Song Practice, and Performance. These things are all based around your song list/repertoire. If you don't have a challenging yet achievable list of songs (somewhere between 2-4 songs), or if you don't have a song list at all, then you need to get one, otherwise your practice is just gonna make you better at practicing, and that's all. Have your songs be congruent: you don't need to be practicing 8 different techniques at once. We've got one more step before we get into the routine:

Song analysis

The key here is to get a quick visual of your songs. Have a look at what techniques are involved. Have a look at their speeds. Know what's in store for you. Find the spots that you can tell are gonna be troublesome for you at your skill level, and know that you're gonna need to spend a little extra practice time on them. Weigh out your practice time with the difficulty of your songs (harder passages get more attention).

Alright, so we've picked a couple of songs. They're totally rad songs with some string skipping, solos heavy with hammer ons and pull offs, and some fast power chord changes. It's at 144 BPM, which is kinda fast given our skill level (those 16th notes). Looks like we've got 3 techniques we need to practice if we're gonna be able to play it well. It's perfect because we can kind of work our way through it (except for maybe one of the licks in the solo). On to our practice routine, which by the way, contains 3 equal parts of practice time. So 10 mins each, 15 mins, or however much time you have to practice divided by 3.

-Step 1: Technique Practice

(This is after our warm-up by the way). Here's where you weigh out the techniques in your song and practice them exclusively. Our song has string skipping in it, so we're gonna find some string-skipping exercises. Our song has hammer-ons and pull-offs, and only a couple of them are really difficult, so we'll only do a bit of hammer-on/pull-off exercises. What's really gonna be tough for us are those power chord changes. We've got 20 minutes of technique practice, so we may want to put 10 minutes into quick power chord changes, and the other 10 minutes divided between the other two techniques. What we're specifically looking to do is find ways to make these exercises easier. Try to analyze our technique and find out what we can do to play the exercises better. Are we relaxed? Are we minimizing motion? You get the idea. This portion is just straight up exercises. We're not worried about the song until:

-Step 2: Song Practice

Here's where we actually pick apart our song. We identify the trouble spots, and try to apply our technique practice to those songs. Our technique practice pays off here because we can actually apply those repetitive, time-cost effective drills to our music. We play our trouble spots over and over for most of the time period, brushing over the easy stuff just to make sure that we've still got our chops up for that, too. The important part here is to apply the same attention to technique that we gave in step 1. If you figured out a good, relaxed way to use your left hand, do the same thing when practicing your song.

-Step 3: Performance (or, the fun part)

Get your recording device ready. For our last third of practice time all we're going to do is perform. Not play, perform. Rock the fuck out. Don't think about your technique or your tone or anything, just perform your beautiful music. Did you flub up the solo? No big deal. We don't need to go back to it. Let's get all the way through our song, because when we're performing there's no saying "oops, sorry crowd, I messed that up. Let me stop, try to play that a couple times, give up, then move on to a different song." We play the whole song for our audience. But luckily, there is no audience except future-us, so let's give them a great show. Play with your soul, not with your mind. Fun is the key word here.

The reason we're just focusing on performing is because, for one thing, performing needs to be practiced just like anything else. But, secondly, when we're not thinking about a passage coming up, or how we're gonna manage it, or stress about how precise our technique is, we often play better. We're more relaxed and we're having more fun.

Now, save the recording of your performance sesh, and play that not right after your performance, but before your next technique practice. We want to end our practice session on a high note, and performing is definitely a high. We're ending with our creative side, not our critical side. We can be critical the next day, and better yet, since we have the recording, we'll have an even better idea of what specific areas we need to work on.

This is an awesome write up!!! I definitely want to emphasize the point you made about powering through your song. There are no re-do's when you're playing live!! I probably make random mistakes at every show. You know what? I realized that the folks on stage are the only ones who know it, and as long as we're all doing a good job of playing follow the leader, the audience is none the wiser, and we'll try not to make the same mistake next time. In a case like mine, where I am the leader, you have to heed the wise words of Captain Nesmith, "Never give up, Never surrender!".. If I stop, the show is over. If I make a mistake, I have to power on and trust that the band will follow.

So today I spoke with someone from a nursing home. My wife has pretty advanced MS, and is mostly bedridden these days. We had been getting by with visiting aides when I'm not home, and they are able to transfer her to her wheelchair/shower using a hoyer lift. But recently that's become too dangerous - in her most recent fall, the leg of the hoyer was bent (not sure if that caused the hoyer to tip, or if her tipping caused the bent leg - whichever it was, the hoyer is now unusable).

It's just too dangerous. I have to go to work, and I can't be there all the time. But one $10/hr bubble-gum popper sitting next to her reading their phone just isn't enough to care for her. My hope was some sort of shared apartment we could both live in - I don't care how small it was, just so that we could live there together and she could get skilled care when I wasn't in. Today I learned that wasn't realistic (at least not with my income - if I win the lottery, all sorts of wonderful options open up for us).

What is going to have to happen is I am going to have to pack up my wife - who isn't even 40 yet - off to a nursing home, where the average age is 85. And, barring any major change of fortune or miracles of medicine, she will never move out.

I don't know how I'm going to bring this up to her. She is going to be so incredibly hurt, scared, angry, and just feel so helpless. Pretty much how I feel.

After the last rounds of home modifications, I thought I was done. I thought no matter how bad she got, I would never let her go. She had been in a nursing home for two "short" stays (3-4 months each time). Although they helped her physically with rehab, they were horrific for her emotionally and spiritually. The people there were wonderful, but she was the youngest person ever to have been admitted there, most days when she wasn't at PT she was just lying in bed. But now our home had a hospital bed, a fully accessible shower/bathroom, we worked our way through Medicare/aide to get her set up with visiting aides, I hooked up her TV to be right over her bed on adjustable arm so it was close enough for her to actually see it (you know, the most important home modification!) - I thought that would be enough.

But now... Now it's not safe for her at home. I can't provide all the care she needs, even with an aide there when I'm not home.

Goddammit. Fuck MS.

Hey,

I just wanted to say that I'm really sorry you're going through this.

My boyfriend is a CNA and is considering contract caregiving in which he goes into homes for an hour at a time. While you may not be able to afford a caregiver full time, would it be helpful to hire someone to come check on her once or twice a day while you're at work? Are there any family or friends who can help out? Have you considered a GoFundMe?

Again, I'm so sorry this is happening to you and your wife. Let's start a dialogue about it and maybe we can come up with, at least, a partial meanwhile solution.

Thanks for the kind words. We actually have aides that are currently with her when I'm at work now, but they're just not skilled enough - last week (for example), she fell out of the hoyer lift (whether it broke before her fall, causing the fall, or after the fall as a result of her falling, we don't know). Her aide couldn't get her off the floor, so I had to come home to get her up. Luckily, she wasn't hurt, but I can only imagine what would have happened had she landed on her back on one of the hoyer's legs!

I feel like a massive failure/monster for not being able to come up with a better plan, but really a home would just be the safest bet at this point. And they would offer physical/occupational therapy, a pool she could get in to with a lift, and activities she could do instead of just lying in bed all day. I know she can't see that right now, but at least in the short term it would help her - maybe in a couple of years I can get this shit-hole of a house fixed up enough to sell for a decent price, and then turn around and buy a condo or one-story house that is way more accessible and she can come back home.

(PS - welcome to the sub!)

It does sound like a home would be better at this point. Good luck to you. If you find you have any questions you can't seem to get answered, let me know and I'll ask my bf, he can ask his DON or the PTs or whatever else. ::huggz::
